claim: Cytoplasmic dynein powers intracellular movement of cargo toward the microtubule minus end.
source: Cytoplasmic dynein powers intracellular movement of cargo toward the microtubule minus end.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about dynein function stated in the abstract and supported by general scientific knowledge.

claim: Two proteins–homologs of Lis1 and Clip170–are sufficient to couple dynein to Kip2, a plus-end-directed kinesin.
source: We find that two proteins–homologs of Lis1 and Clip170–are sufficient to couple dynein to Kip2, a plus-end-directed kinesin.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the reconstitution experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Dynein is transported to the plus end by Kip2, but is not a passive passenger, resisting its own plus-end-directed motion.
source: Dynein is transported to the plus end by Kip2, but is not a passive passenger, resisting its own plus-end-directed motion.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data showing that weakening dynein's microtubule affinity increases its plus-end velocity.

claim: Two microtubule-associated proteins, homologs of Clip170 and EB1, act as processivity factors for Kip2.
source: Two microtubule-associated proteins, homologs of Clip170 and EB1, act as processivity factors for Kip2, helping it overcome dynein's intrinsic minus-end-directed motility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing increased Kip2 run length in the presence of Bik1 and Bim1.

claim: Dynein accumulates at the plus ends of microtubules in diverse organisms.
source: Live-cell imaging in diverse organisms reveals that, surprisingly for a minus-end-directed motor, dynein accumulates at the plus ends of microtubules that grow and shrink near the cell periphery (Vaughan et al., 1999; Han et al., 2001; Ma and Chisholm, 2002; Lee et al., 2003; Sheeman et al., 2003; Lenz et al., 2006; Kobayashi and Murayama, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Dynein uses the energy from ATP hydrolysis to move cargoes toward the minus end of microtubules.
source: Cytoplasmic dynein, a large and complex AAA+ motor protein (Carter, 2013), uses the energy from ATP hydrolysis to move cargoes toward the minus end of microtubules (typically toward the cell center).
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynein's mechanism, supported by a citation.

claim: Dynein can act while anchored at the cell cortex, where it pulls the microtubule network toward it.
source: In addition, dyneins can act while anchored at the cell cortex, where they pull the microtubule network toward them (Moore et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The targeting of the dynein machinery to the microtubule plus end is crucial for proper dynein function in budding yeast.
source: The targeting of the dynein machinery to the microtubule plus end is crucial for proper dynein function in budding yeast (Moore et al., 2009), filamentous fungi (Wu et al., 2006), and a subset of metazoan cells, including mammalian neurons (Lomakin et al., 2009; Lloyd et al., 2012; Moughamian and Holzbaur, 2012; Moughamian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: EBs (end-binding proteins) preferentially bind to unique structural features present at the plus end vs the body of the microtubule.
source: First, a subset of +TIPs preferentially bind to unique structural features present at the plus end vs the body of the microtubule, and can recruit additional proteins to these sites. The prototypical example of this class of +TIP are EBs (end-binding proteins), which are involved in recruiting binding partners such as Clip170 and the dynein regulator dynactin to plus ends in metazoans (Watson and Stephens, 2006; Bieling et al., 2007; Dixit et al., 2009; Zanic et al., 2009; Maurer et al., 2012; Moughamian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing EB protein function.

claim: Kinesin motor proteins can power the vectorial transport of proteins along the microtubule body to the plus end.
source: Second, kinesin motor proteins can power the vectorial transport of proteins along the microtubule body to the plus end (Bieling et al., 2007; Subramanian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, genetic studies implicate at least three proteins in targeting dynein to the microtubule plus end: Lis1, Bik1, and Kip2.
source: In the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, genetic studies implicate at least three proteins in targeting dynein to the microtubule plus end: Lis1, a regulator of dynein motility (Lee et al., 2003; Sheeman et al., 2003); Bik1, a homolog of Clip170 (Sheeman et al., 2003; Markus et al., 2009); and Kip2, a plus-end-directed kinesin motor (Carvalho et al., 2004; Caudron et al., 2008; Markus et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to genetic studies.

claim: Deletion of the EB homolog (Bim1) in S. cerevisiae appears to have little effect on the plus-end targeting of dynein and its co-factors.
source: Deletion of the EB homolog (Bim1) in S. cerevisiae appears to have little effect on the plus-end targeting of dynein and its co-factors (Carvalho et al., 2004; Caudron et al., 2008; Markus et al., 2011), despite (1) Bim1 binding directly to Bik1, an essential factor for dynein plus-end targeting (Sheeman et al., 2003; Blake-Hodek et al., 2010); and (2) The homologs of Kip2, Bik1 and Bim1 functioning together as a plus-end tracking system in fission yeast (Bieling et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: S. cerevisiae dynein is a forceful minus-end-directed motor with constitutive activity in motility assays.
source: This problem is particularly pressing for S. cerevisiae dynein: a forceful minus-end-directed motor with constitutive activity in motility assays (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006; Gennerich et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous motility studies.

claim: Kip2 from S. cerevisiae migrates as a doublet of bands corresponding to differently phosphorylated isoforms.
source: Each purified protein migrated as a single band by SDS-PAGE (Figure 1A) with the exception of Kip2, which migrated as a doublet. The Kip2 bands correspond to differently phosphorylated forms of the protein; after treatment with λ phosphatase, the Kip2 doublet collapsed into a single band (Figure 1A, inset).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phosphatase treatment experiment shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Dynein and Lis1 co-elute as a complex in size-exclusion chromatography.
source: Dynein and Lis1 co-elute in a complex, as verified by SDS-PAGE of the fractions (Figure 1B; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown by size-exclusion chromatography data in Figure 1B and supported by a citation.

claim: Bik1, Bim1 and Kip2 co-elute in a ternary complex.
source: We also found that Bik1, Bim1 and Kip2 co-elute in a ternary complex (Figure 1B), resembling the behavior of related proteins from Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Bieling et al., 2007; Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by size-exclusion chromatography data in Figure 1B.

claim: A pair-wise mixture of Kip2 with Bim1 did not elute as a complex under the same conditions.
source: A pair-wise mixture of Kip2 with Bim1 did not elute as a complex under the same conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Bim1 binds with higher affinity to the Kip2-Bik1 complex.
evidence: This is shown by size-exclusion chromatography data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bim1 binds with higher affinity to the Kip2-Bik1 complex than to Kip2 alone.
source: A pair-wise mixture of Kip2 with Bim1 did not elute as a complex under the same conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Bim1 binds with higher affinity to the Kip2-Bik1 complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Bim1 and Kip2 do not co-elute alone but do co-elute when Bik1 is present.

claim: Dynein-Lis1 and Bik1-Bim1-Kip2 each form complexes that are sufficiently stable to co-elute by size-exclusion chromatography.
source: In summary, these first experiments with all five purified components demonstrate that dynein-Lis1 and Bik1-Bim1-Kip2 each form complexes that are sufficiently stable to co-elute by size-exclusion chromatography.
evidence: This is a summary of the size-exclusion chromatography data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The dynein-Lis1 and Bik1-Bim1-Kip2 sub-complexes did not stably associate in solution.
source: Given that the dynein-Lis1 and Bik1-Bim1-Kip2 sub-complexes did not stably associate in solution (Figure 1B), we hypothesized that these two assemblies might interact dynamically on the microtubule.
evidence: This is shown by size-exclusion chromatography data in Figure 1B.

claim: Wild-type dynein binds strongly to the microtubule in the absence of nucleotide.
source: When wild-type dynein is mixed with microtubules in the absence of nucleotide, it binds strongly to the microtubule, as visualized by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy in Figure 1C (lane 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Four mutations in dynein's microtubule-binding domain (K3116A, K3117A, E3122A, R3124A) severely weaken its association with microtubules.
source: In order to monitor dynein recruitment to the microtubule by other proteins, we introduced four mutations into its microtubule-binding domain (Koonce and Tikhonenko, 2000; Carter et al., 2008; Redwine et al., 2012), which severely weakened its association with microtubules (Figure 1C, lane 2; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Weak-binding dynein can be recruited efficiently to the microtubule by the combined presence of Lis1, Bik1, Kip2 and Bim1.
source: However, the weak-binding dynein could be recruited efficiently to the microtubule by the combined presence of Lis1, Bik1, Kip2 and Bim1 (Figure 1C, lane 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dynein recruitment to microtubules depends strictly on the presence of Lis1 and Bik1.
source: This dynein recruitment depended strictly on the presence of Lis1 and Bik1 (Figure 1C, lanes 4 and 5), consistent with the idea that Lis1 and Bik1/Clip170 interact directly (Coquelle et al., 2002; Sheeman et al., 2003; Lansbergen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and supported by citations.

claim: Lis1 and Bik1/Clip170 interact directly.
source: This dynein recruitment depended strictly on the presence of Lis1 and Bik1 (Figure 1C, lanes 4 and 5), consistent with the idea that Lis1 and Bik1/Clip170 interact directly (Coquelle et al., 2002; Sheeman et al., 2003; Lansbergen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bik1ΔC construct lacking the C-terminal region retained the ability to bind Kip2 and Bim1.
source: The Bik1ΔC construct retained the ability to bind Kip2 and Bim1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by size-exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bik1ΔC construct's ability to recruit weak-dynein to the microtubule in the presence of Lis1, Kip2 and Bim1 was abolished.
source: However, its ability to recruit the weak-dynein to the microtubule in the presence of Lis1, Kip2 and Bim1 was abolished (Figure 1C, lane 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dynein-Lis1 and Bik1-Bim1-Kip2 interact in a manner dependent on Lis1 and the C-terminal region of Bik1.
source: Together, these results suggest that dynein-Lis1 and Bik1-Bim1-Kip2 each form sub-complexes, which in turn interact in a manner dependent on Lis1 and the C-terminal region of Bik1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Bik1ΔC cannot recruit dynein.

claim: Dynein moved toward the minus end of the microtubule in the absence of Lis1, Bik1, and Bim1.
source: In the absence of Lis1, Bik1, and Bim1, dynein moved toward the minus end of the microtubule, and Kip2 moved toward the plus end, as expected (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic microtubule assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Kip2 moved toward the plus end of the microtubule in the absence of Lis1, Bik1, and Bim1.
source: In the absence of Lis1, Bik1, and Bim1, dynein moved toward the minus end of the microtubule, and Kip2 moved toward the plus end, as expected (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic microtubule assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Dynein has the intrinsic ability to track dynamic microtubule minus ends.
source: Notably, upon reaching the minus end of the microtubule, dynein accumulated at, and moved with, the slowly growing end of the polymer (Figure 2B). Dynein showed the same behavior in the absence of Kip2, indicating that dynein has the intrinsic ability to track dynamic microtubule minus ends.
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic microtubule assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the presence of Lis1, Bik1, Bim1 and Kip2, the large majority of dynein movements along the body of the microtubule were directed to the plus end.
source: Strikingly, in the presence of Lis1, Bik1, Bim1 and Kip2, the large majority of dynein movements along the body of the microtubule were directed to the plus end (Figure 2C, lane 1) (90 ± 3%; proportion ± SE, N = 122).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic microtubule assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: On 63 ± 7% of microtubules, dynein was present at the growing plus end itself in the presence of Lis1, Bik1, Bim1 and Kip2.
source: Moreover, on 63 ± 7% of microtubules, dynein was present at the growing plus end itself (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), reminiscent of dynein localization in living yeast cells (Lee et al., 2003; Sheeman et al., 2003; Markus et al., 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic microtubule assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A system of four proteins (Lis1, Bik1, Bim1, and Kip2) is sufficient to strongly bias dynein's movement toward the microtubule plus end.
source: Thus, we conclude that a system of four proteins (Lis1, Bik1, Bim1, and Kip2) is sufficient to strongly bias dynein's movement toward the microtubule plus end.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reconstitution experiments with purified proteins.

claim: Dynein's plus-end-directed motion depended strictly on Kip2.
source: Dynein's plus-end-directed motion depended strictly on Kip2 (Figure 2C, lane 5), but was slower than that of free Kip2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), leading us to hypothesize that dynein might have the capacity to resist its own transport to the plus end.
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic microtubule assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Dynein's plus-end-directed motion was slower than that of free Kip2.
source: Dynein's plus-end-directed motion depended strictly on Kip2 (Figure 2C, lane 5), but was slower than that of free Kip2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), leading us to hypothesize that dynein might have the capacity to resist its own transport to the plus end.
evidence: This is demonstrated by velocity measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The plus-end velocity of the weak-binding dynein was increased relative to the wild-type protein, becoming close to that of Kip2.
source: Strikingly, the plus-end velocity of the weak-binding dynein was increased relative to the wild-type protein, becoming close to that of Kip2 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by velocity measurements shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The weak-binding dynein showed strong accumulation at the plus end of the microtubule.
source: Moreover, the weak-binding dynein also showed strong accumulation at the plus end of the microtubule (Figure 2C, lane 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic microtubule assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Wild-type dynein is not a passive passenger during its plus-end-directed transport.
source: These results indicate that wild-type dynein is not a passive passenger during its plus-end-directed transport.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that weakening dynein's microtubule affinity increases its plus-end velocity.

claim: Wild-type dynein and Kip2 have the potential to engage simultaneously with the microtubule in a 'tug-of-war'-like mechanism.
source: Instead, the data support a model in which wild-type dynein and Kip2 have the potential to engage simultaneously with the microtubule in a 'tug-of-war'-like mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the velocity data showing that dynein can resist its transport by Kip2.

claim: Weak dynein construct frequently localized with Kip2 midway through a run, and dissociated before its end.
source: Notably, the dynein construct frequently localized with Kip2 midway through a run, and dissociated before its end, consistent with transient binding as indicated by our biochemical experiments (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The movement of dynein toward the plus end is driven directly by Kip2.
source: These observations suggest that the movement of dynein toward the plus end is driven directly by Kip2.
evidence: This is inferred from colocalization data showing dynein and Kip2 moving together.

claim: Lis1 and Bik1 are critical for dynein's plus-end-directed movement.
source: Lis1 and Bik1 were critical for dynein's plus-end-directed movement (Figure 2C, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dropout experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the absence of Lis1 or Bik1, dynein moved to the minus end of the microtubule, despite the continued movement of Kip2 to the plus end.
source: In their absence, dynein moved to the minus end of the microtubule, despite the continued movement of Kip2 to the plus end.
evidence: This is demonstrated by dropout experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lis1 and Bik1 are required to connect dynein to Kip2.
source: These results indicate that Lis1 and Bik1 are required to connect dynein to Kip2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dynein moves to the minus end in the absence of Lis1 or Bik1.

claim: Omitting Kip2 abolished dynein's plus-end-directed movement.
source: Omitting Kip2 abolished dynein's plus-end-directed movement, showing that the pathway we have reconstituted is kinesin dependent (Figure 2C, lane 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dropout experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Removal of Kip2 increased the frequency of microtubule catastrophes.
source: Interestingly, removal of Kip2 also increased the frequency of microtubule catastrophes (the conversion from growth to shrinkage; Figure 2C, arrows), consistent with the short microtubule phenotype caused by Kip2 deletion in vivo (Cottingham and Hoyt, 1997).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic microtubule assay data shown in Figure 2C and supported by a citation.

claim: In the absence of Bim1, dynein could still be transported to the plus end, but the fraction of plus- vs minus-end-directed dynein movements was roughly balanced.
source: Finally, we observed an unexpected influence of Bim1 (Figure 2C, lane 6). In the absence of Bim1, dynein could still be transported to the plus end, but the fraction of plus- vs minus-end-directed dynein movements was roughly balanced (47 vs 53 ± 5%, respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dropout experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lis1, Bik1 and Kip2 constitute the minimal machinery for transporting dynein to the plus end.
source: Thus, Lis1, Bik1 and Kip2 constitute the minimal machinery for transporting dynein to the plus end, and Bim1 can regulate this machinery to increase the fraction of dynein movements that are directed to the plus end.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dropout experiments.

claim: Bim1 can regulate the dynein transport machinery to increase the fraction of dynein movements that are directed to the plus end.
source: Thus, Lis1, Bik1 and Kip2 constitute the minimal machinery for transporting dynein to the plus end, and Bim1 can regulate this machinery to increase the fraction of dynein movements that are directed to the plus end.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dropout experiments showing Bim1's effect on directionality.

claim: There is an SxIP motif within an extension N-terminal to the kinesin motor domain of Kip2.
source: Furthermore, analysis of the Kip2 amino acid sequence revealed that there is an SxIP motif within an extension N-terminal to the kinesin motor domain (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of Kip2.

claim: The SxIP motif is a signature sequence that interacts with EB-family proteins such as Bim1.
source: The SxIP motif is a signature sequence that interacts with EB-family proteins such as Bim1 (Honnappa et al., 2009), suggesting that Bim1 may interact with Kip2 through this motif.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on SxIP motifs.

claim: Bim1 binds to the Cap-Gly domain of Bik1.
source: Bim1 also binds to the Cap-Gly domain of Bik1 (Blake-Hodek et al., 2010) and the microtubule lattice (Zimniak et al., 2009), while Bik1's coiled coil is thought to interact with Kip2 (Newman et al., 2000; Carvalho et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Bim1 binds to the microtubule lattice.
source: Bim1 also binds to the Cap-Gly domain of Bik1 (Blake-Hodek et al., 2010) and the microtubule lattice (Zimniak et al., 2009), while Bik1's coiled coil is thought to interact with Kip2 (Newman et al., 2000; Carvalho et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Bik1's coiled coil is thought to interact with Kip2.
source: Bim1 also binds to the Cap-Gly domain of Bik1 (Blake-Hodek et al., 2010) and the microtubule lattice (Zimniak et al., 2009), while Bik1's coiled coil is thought to interact with Kip2 (Newman et al., 2000; Carvalho et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the absence of regulators, the average distance traveled by Kip2 per microtubule encounter was 1.2 ± 0.1 μm.
source: In the absence of regulators, the average distance traveled by Kip2 per microtubule encounter was 1.2 ± 0.1 μm (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-molecule motility assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The addition of Bik1 or Bim1 individually had minor effects on Kip2 run length.
source: The addition of Bik1 or Bim1 individually had minor effects on Kip2 run length.
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-molecule motility assays shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: In the presence of both Bik1 and Bim1, the run length of Kip2 increased fourfold, to 4.8 ± 0.3 μm.
source: However, in the presence of both Bik1 and Bim1, the run length of Kip2 increased fourfold, to 4.8 ± 0.3 μm (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-molecule motility assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a small decrease in Kip2 velocity in the presence of both Bik1 and Bim1.
source: Concomitantly, there was a small decrease in Kip2 velocity, while the Kip2 copy number (judged by fluorescence intensity per spot) was unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by velocity measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Kip2 copy number (judged by fluorescence intensity per spot) was unchanged in the presence of both Bik1 and Bim1.
source: Concomitantly, there was a small decrease in Kip2 velocity, while the Kip2 copy number (judged by fluorescence intensity per spot) was unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bik1 and Bim1 had minimal effects on dynein motility.
source: These effects were specific to Kip2: Bik1 and Bim1 had minimal effects on dynein motility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by motility assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bik1 and Bim1 increase the on-rate and reduce the off-rate of Kip2's microtubule encounters.
source: Analysis of Kip2 landing events and run durations revealed that Bik1 and Bim1 increase the on-rate and reduce the off-rate of Kip2's microtubule encounters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that these factors augment Kip2's microtubule affinity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of landing events and run durations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bik1 and Bim1 augment Kip2's microtubule affinity.
source: Analysis of Kip2 landing events and run durations revealed that Bik1 and Bim1 increase the on-rate and reduce the off-rate of Kip2's microtubule encounters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that these factors augment Kip2's microtubule affinity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Bik1 and Bim1 increase on-rate and reduce off-rate.

claim: Bik1 and Bim1 together act as processivity factors for Kip2.
source: In summary, we conclude that Bik1 and Bim1 together act as processivity factors for Kip2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the motility data showing increased run length.

claim: The large majority (80 ± 2%; mean ± SEM) of dynein/Kip2-chassis movements on the microtubule were in the minus-end (dynein) direction.
source: Under this regime, the large majority (80 ± 2%; mean ± SEM) of dynein/Kip2-chassis movements on the microtubule were in the minus-end (dynein) direction, as visualized by the incorporation of fluorescently labeled DNA strands (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA origami chassis experiments shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Chassis-coupled motors were in a tug-of-war: both minus- and plus-end-directed runs exhibited reduced velocity compared to single-motor chassis.
source: Velocity analysis indicated that the chassis-coupled motors were in a tug-of-war: both minus- and plus-end-directed runs exhibited reduced velocity compared to single-motor chassis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by velocity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of either Bik1 or Bim1 alone had a modest effect on the motility of the dynein/Kip2-chassis complex.
source: The addition of either Bik1 or Bim1 alone had a modest effect on the motility of the dynein/Kip2-chassis complex: the fraction of minus- and plus-end-directed runs was changed little (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA origami chassis experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Inclusion of Bik1 and Bim1 together caused the fraction of plus-end-directed runs to markedly increase.
source: In contrast, inclusion of Bik1 and Bim1 together caused the fraction of plus-end-directed runs to markedly increase (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA origami chassis experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the presence of Bik1 and Bim1, the dynein/Kip2-chassis underwent switches in direction during a run (10 ± 1% of events).
source: Under these conditions, the dynein/Kip2-chassis also underwent switches in direction during a run (Figure 4B; orange trace; 10 ± 1% of events).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA origami chassis experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Regulatory proteins can tune the outcome of a tug-of-war between dynein and the kinesin Kip2.
source: These results reveal that regulatory proteins can tune the outcome of a tug-of-war between dynein and the kinesin Kip2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DNA origami chassis experiments.

claim: The connection between dynein and Kip2 is capable of bearing load on the microtubule.
source: This connection is capable of bearing load on the microtubule, but is not stable enough to be observed by size-exclusion chromatography.
evidence: This is inferred from the tug-of-war experiments and the lack of stable complex formation in solution.

claim: The connection between dynein and Kip2 is not stable enough to be observed by size-exclusion chromatography.
source: This connection is capable of bearing load on the microtubule, but is not stable enough to be observed by size-exclusion chromatography.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the size-exclusion chromatography data in Figure 1B.

claim: A high off-rate between dynein and Kip2 might allow for dynamic regulation.
source: As is the case for interactions found in other self-organizing systems (Kirschner et al., 2000), a high off-rate between dynein and Kip2 might allow for dynamic regulation, for example enabling dynein to readily detach from Kip2 following targeting.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed transient interaction and supported by a citation.

claim: The timescale of dynein 'offloading' from the microtubule plus end onto its receptor on the cell cortex is on the order of seconds in vivo.
source: Indeed, in vivo, the timescale of dynein 'offloading' from the microtubule plus end onto its receptor on the cell cortex is on the order of seconds (Markus and Lee, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Lis1's ß-propeller domain binds to the AAA4 subdomain of dynein's motor domain.
source: Specifically, Lis1's ß-propeller domain binds to the AAA4 subdomain of dynein's motor domain (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The dynein/Lis1 complex interacts dynamically with the C-terminal zinc-knuckle domain of Bik1/Clip170.
source: The dynein/Lis1 complex interacts dynamically with the C-terminal zinc-knuckle domain of Bik1/Clip170 (Coquelle et al., 2002; Sheeman et al., 2003; Lansbergen et al., 2004; Markus et al., 2011) as indicated by the double arrow.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The C-terminal tail of Bim1 likely interacts with the N-terminal Cap-Gly domain of Bik1.
source: As depicted with dotted lines, it is likely that the C-terminal tail of Bim1 interacts with the N-terminal Cap-Gly domain of Bik1 (Weisbrich et al., 2007), and the cargo-binding domain of Bim1 interacts with the SxIP motif of Kip2 (Honnappa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The cargo-binding domain of Bim1 likely interacts with the SxIP motif of Kip2.
source: As depicted with dotted lines, it is likely that the C-terminal tail of Bim1 interacts with the N-terminal Cap-Gly domain of Bik1 (Weisbrich et al., 2007), and the cargo-binding domain of Bim1 interacts with the SxIP motif of Kip2 (Honnappa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The calponin-homology domain of Bim1 is likely free to interact transiently with the microtubule lattice.
source: This arrangement would leave the calponin-homolgy domain of Bim1 (Slep and Vale, 2007) free to interact transiently with the microtubule lattice, and thus promote Kip2's microtubule association.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed arrangement of interactions and supported by a citation.

claim: The SxIP motif of Kip2 is flanked by serine residues that can be phosphorylated.
source: The SxIP motif is flanked by serine residues (blue) that can be phosphorylated (Holt et al., 2009; Bodenmiller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The addition and removal of phosphate groups on the N-terminal extension of Kip2's motor domain has the potential to influence its interaction with Bim1.
source: Specifically, the addition and removal of phosphate groups on the N-terminal extension of Kip2's motor domain has the potential to influence its interaction with Bim1 (Figure 3A; Honnappa et al., 2009), as well as the negatively charged microtubule surface, both of which could impact Kip2 motility.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the presence of phosphorylation sites and supported by a citation.

claim: The high local concentration of Lis1 at plus ends in S. cerevisiae may help retain dynein by prolonging its microtubule attachments.
source: Once dynein reaches the plus end, the high local concentration of Lis1 at plus ends in S. cerevisiae (Markus et al., 2011) may help retain dynein by prolonging its microtubule attachments (Huang et al., 2012; McKenney et al., 2010; Yamada et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Nudel may promote dynein plus-end targeting by tethering Lis1 to dynein.
source: Nudel, a Lis1 and dynein binding partner, may also promote dynein plus-end targeting by tethering Lis1 to dynein (Li et al., 2005; McKenney et al., 2010; Wang and Zheng, 2011; Zylkiewicz et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Genetic studies indicate there is a second pathway for targeting dynein directly from the cytoplasm to the plus end that does not require Kip2.
source: Notably, genetic studies indicate there is a second pathway for targeting dynein directly from the cytoplasm to the plus end that does not require Kip2 (Caudron et al., 2008; Markus et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: Overlap between dynein targeting pathways in vivo may explain why Bim1's capacity to regulate dynein plus-end transport was previously hidden.
source: Overlap between these pathways in vivo may explain why Bim1's capacity to regulate dynein plus-end transport was previously hidden.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the existence of multiple pathways.

claim: The dynein construct used lacks the cargo-binding tail, which is dispensable for plus-end targeting in vivo.
source: This dynein construct lacks the cargo-binding tail, which is dispensable for plus-end targeting in vivo (Markus et al., 2009), and is dimerized by GST to yield a motor with highly-similar motile properties to full-length dynein (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.
